meta.title: [IRS] Quiz 7 — Language Models & Query Expansion
meta.description: Dirichlet/JM smoothing, PRF, RM3, WordNet expansion, vocabulary mismatch.

questions.questionMd: According to Week 7, what is **topic drift** in the context of Pseudo-Relevance Feedback, and when is it most likely to occur?

options.label: A
options.text: Topic drift occurs when the Dirichlet smoothing parameter mu is set too high during the initial retrieval pass, making all document scores converge toward the collection model and causing the top-k results to be drawn from an unrelated region of the collection.

options.label: B
options.text: Topic drift occurs when the PRF expansion adds too many terms that already appear in the original query, causing the expanded query to retrieve the same documents as the original query without any improvement in precision or recall across the evaluation queries.

options.label: C
options.text: Topic drift occurs when the top-k retrieved documents cluster on a specific subtopic of the query, causing the extracted expansion terms to reinforce that subtopic rather than the broader information need, and is most likely for short, ambiguous queries with poor initial retrieval precision.

options.label: D
options.text: Topic drift occurs when the Rocchio beta parameter is set lower than 0.5, causing the expanded query to weight the original query terms more heavily than the pseudo-relevant centroid and thereby failing to incorporate any new concepts from the feedback documents.

questions.explanationMd: In PRF, expansion terms are extracted from the initially retrieved top-k documents. If those documents represent only one sense or subtopic of an ambiguous query, the expansion can reinforce that wrong/narrow sense and move the query away from the original information need.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture briefly previews neural query expansion using Word2Vec or GloVe embeddings. How do these embedding-based methods find expansion terms differently from co-occurrence-based MI expansion?

options.label: A
options.text: Word2Vec and GloVe find expansion terms by running a secondary BM25 retrieval pass over a large background corpus and selecting the terms with the highest BM25 scores across that background corpus as candidates to add to the original query.

options.label: B
options.text: Word2Vec and GloVe find expansion terms by consulting a pre-built WordNet synset dictionary in which each word's neighbors are its definitional synonyms, providing a curated lexical database that is independent of the document collection being searched.

options.label: C
options.text: Word2Vec and GloVe find expansion terms by computing the Rocchio centroid in embedding space rather than TF-IDF space, applying exactly the same geometric update formula but replacing the TF-IDF vectors of each document with their corresponding pre-trained embeddings.

options.label: D
options.text: Word2Vec and GloVe find expansion terms by identifying nearest neighbors in a dense vector embedding space, capturing semantic similarity based on distributional context without requiring explicit co-occurrence counts between the query term and candidate expansion terms in the same document.

questions.explanationMd: Embedding-based expansion uses vector-space semantic similarity. Terms close to the query term in a dense embedding space can be chosen as expansion terms even if they did not explicitly co-occur with the query term in the same retrieved documents.

questions.questionMd: The lecture identifies two broad solution families for the vocabulary mismatch problem. Which of the following correctly describes both families as presented in Week 7?

options.label: A
options.text: Inverted index compression, which reduces the cost of scanning many postings lists for synonym terms; and user query reformulation, which prompts users to rewrite their query in more document-like language.

options.label: B
options.text: BM25 parameter tuning, which adjusts k1 and b so that documents containing near-synonyms are ranked higher; and neural reranking, which reorders BM25 results using a pretrained embedding model.

options.label: C
options.text: Document expansion, which rewrites stored documents to include synonyms at retrieval time; and stemming normalization, which reduces all query and document terms to a shared root form before matching.

options.label: D
options.text: Probabilistic LM which reframes document scoring so that unseen query terms receive small but non-zero probability; and query expansion, which adds related terms to the query before retrieval is performed.

questions.explanationMd: Week 7 frames vocabulary mismatch through two major approaches: language-model smoothing, which gives unseen terms small non-zero probabilities, and query expansion, which adds related terms before retrieval.

questions.questionMd: According to the Week 7 lecture, what is the practical relationship between the Dirichlet-smoothed language model and BM25 in terms of retrieval behavior?

options.label: A
options.text: BM25 is strictly a special case of the Dirichlet language model, obtained by setting mu equal to k1 and setting the length normalization parameter b to the ratio of the average document length to the collection size.

options.label: B
options.text: The Dirichlet language model and BM25 are fundamentally incompatible scoring paradigms whose results can't be compared numerically because one produces probabilities while the other produces unnormalized heuristic scores.

options.label: C
options.text: The Dirichlet language model consistently and substantially outperforms BM25 across all standard retrieval benchmarks because it is derived from principled Bayesian probability theory rather than from empirical heuristics about term weighting.

options.label: D
options.text: The Dirichlet language model approximates BM25 under certain parameter settings, since both models reward term frequency and penalize document length, and their empirical retrieval performance on TREC benchmarks is typically very similar.

questions.explanationMd: Although BM25 and Dirichlet language modeling come from different formulations, both reward term frequency and include document-length normalization effects. In practice, their retrieval behavior can be similar under suitable parameter choices.

questions.questionMd: What is the polysemy problem in the context of WordNet-based global query expansion, as described in Week 7, and which mitigation strategy is mentioned in the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Polysemy means the WordNet thesaurus does not cover technical or domain-specific vocabulary, so expansion terms generated from the thesaurus are frequently absent from the document collection and contribute no additional retrieval signal.

options.label: B
options.text: Polysemy means that synonyms from the thesaurus are too general and frequently appear in almost every document in the collection, which reduces their discriminative power and causes expanded queries to retrieve many irrelevant documents.

options.label: C
options.text: Polysemy means a query term has multiple senses, so a thesaurus expansion may add synonyms for the wrong sense and hurt precision. A mitigation is to expand only low-frequency query terms or to skip terms that appear in too many synset groups.

options.label: D
options.text: Polysemy means two different query terms share the same synonym, causing the expansion to add duplicate terms to the query that inflate the weight of a single concept and introduce a bias toward documents that happen to contain that synonym.

questions.explanationMd: Polysemy means one word can have multiple meanings. If WordNet expansion picks synonyms for the wrong sense, precision can drop. The lecture's mitigation is to avoid risky/highly ambiguous terms, such as terms that appear in too many synsets.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture uses the query **"jaguar"** to illustrate topic drift during PRF. Which scenario correctly describes how topic drift manifests for this query?

options.label: A
options.text: The Dirichlet smoothing parameter mu is set too low for the "jaguar" query, causing the initial retrieval to assign zero probability to many automotive-related terms and preventing the PRF system from finding any meaningful expansion terms at all.

options.label: B
options.text: If the initial top-k results are dominated by automotive reviews, the expansion terms will be concepts like "horsepower", "engine", and "sedan", causing the re-retrieved results to further emphasize the car sense of "jaguar" and crowd out wildlife or other relevant concepts.

options.label: C
options.text: If the initial top-k results are dominated by wildlife articles, the expansion terms will be concepts like "prey", "habitat", and "feline", which are highly specific synonyms that narrow the query to only wildlife documents and exclude many other relevant automotive sources.

options.label: D
options.text: The WordNet thesaurus assigns "jaguar" to a single unambiguous synset covering only the animal sense, so all expansion terms from the thesaurus refer to wildlife, and the RM3 model fails to find documents about Jaguar cars regardless of the initial retrieval results.

questions.explanationMd: For an ambiguous query like `jaguar`, PRF can overfit to the sense represented in the initial top-k results. If those results are about cars, car-related terms are added and the next retrieval round drifts further toward the automotive sense.

questions.questionMd: Week 7 explains that Jelinek-Mercer smoothing has a specific weakness compared to Dirichlet smoothing for ad-hoc information retrieval. What is this weakness?

options.label: A
options.text: JM smoothing cannot assign non-zero probability to terms that are absent from a document, because the linear interpolation formula reduces to zero for unseen terms when the collection model probability P(t|C) is itself zero for out-of-vocabulary terms.

options.label: B
options.text: JM smoothing assigns higher probability to unseen terms in long documents than in short documents, creating an undesirable bias toward longer documents that inflates their scores for multi-term queries compared to shorter documents on the same topic.

options.label: C
options.text: JM smoothing requires a separate optimization step to estimate the optimal lambda value for each individual document, making it computationally more expensive than Dirichlet smoothing, which uses a single shared mu parameter across all documents in the collection.

options.label: D
options.text: JM smoothing uses a fixed lambda for all documents regardless of their length, so a short document and a long document receive the same degree of collection-model smoothing, whereas Dirichlet adapts the smoothing amount based on document length.

questions.explanationMd: Jelinek-Mercer uses a fixed interpolation parameter, so the smoothing amount is not automatically adjusted according to document length. Dirichlet smoothing adapts because document length and `mu` jointly determine the relative influence of the document model and collection model.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture distinguishes between global and local query expansion strategies. Which of the following correctly characterizes the key difference between these two approaches?

options.label: A
options.text: Global expansion is applied to all terms in a query simultaneously using a single expansion dictionary, whereas local expansion is applied selectively to only those query terms that receive fewer than a minimum threshold number of matching documents.

options.label: B
options.text: Global expansion modifies the document index by adding synonyms at indexing time before queries arrive, whereas local expansion modifies the query at search time by adding terms derived only from the query string itself without consulting retrieved documents.

options.label: C
options.text: Global expansion uses fixed, collection-wide resources such as thesauri or co-occurrence statistics that are independent of any particular query, whereas local expansion derives expansion terms from the top-k retrieved results of the current query being processed.

options.label: D
options.text: Global expansion uses the full document collection as a retrieval source for expansion terms, whereas local expansion restricts the source of expansion terms to a small curated subset of documents manually selected by a domain expert.

questions.explanationMd: Global expansion relies on resources prepared independently of the specific query, such as thesauri or precomputed co-occurrence statistics. Local expansion uses the current query's retrieved results, typically the top-k documents, to select expansion terms.

questions.questionMd: The unigram language model used in Week 7 rests on an independence assumption about how words in a document are generated. What is this assumption, and what is one consequence of making it?

options.label: A
options.text: Words are assumed to be drawn uniformly from the vocabulary, so every word in the document has the same probability and the model only needs the vocabulary size to compute any term's probability in any document.

options.label: B
options.text: Words are assumed to depend only on the immediately preceding word, so the joint probability of a word sequence is computed as a chain of bigram conditional probabilities. This is the same as assuming a first-order Markov model for language generation.

options.label: C
options.text: Words are assumed to be generated independently of each other, so the joint probability of a word sequence is the product of individual word probabilities. This makes the model computationally tractable but means word order is completely ignored.

options.label: D
options.text: Words are assumed to depend on all preceding words in the document, so the joint probability of a word sequence is computed as a product of full-history conditional probabilities, which is the most accurate but computationally intractable formulation.

questions.explanationMd: A unigram language model treats words as independent draws from a document language model. This enables simple multiplication of term probabilities but ignores ordering and phrase structure.

questions.questionMd: During the Week 7 lab, a student notices that all DirichletLM retrieval scores are nearly identical regardless of which document is being scored. According to the troubleshooting guide, what is the most likely cause of this problem?

options.label: A
options.text: The mu parameter is set too high, causing every document's term probabilities to collapse toward the collection model P(t|C). When mu greatly exceeds all document lengths, the denominator |d| + mu is dominated by mu and all documents produce essentially the same smoothed probabilities.

options.label: B
options.text: The stop word list was not applied to the TfidfVectorizer, causing high-frequency function words to dominate the expansion terms and produce centroids that are nearly identical across all documents regardless of their topic or category.

options.label: C
options.text: The doc_probs vector used in the RM3 computation has not been normalized by dividing by its sum, causing all document relevance weights to be inflated by a factor equal to the sum of raw BM25 scores and making the final P(t|R) values sum to much more than 1.0.

options.label: D
options.text: The expanded query from the PRF step is being passed back into the original unsmoothed MLE scorer rather than the DirichletLM scorer, so document-specific term frequencies are ignored and all documents receive a score proportional only to query term lengths.

questions.explanationMd: If `mu` is much larger than document lengths, the collection model dominates the smoothed probability estimate for every document. As a result, scores become nearly identical because document-specific evidence has little influence.

questions.questionMd: One key advantage of Dirichlet smoothing over Jelinek-Mercer smoothing highlighted in Week 7 is that Dirichlet smoothing is adaptive to document length. What does this mean in practice?

options.label: A
options.text: Both short and long documents receive exactly the same degree of smoothing because the mu parameter appears in both the numerator and denominator and cancels out algebraically when computing the ratio.

options.label: B
options.text: Short documents receive heavier smoothing toward the collection model because |d| is much smaller than mu, so the denominator is dominated by mu and the collection prior has a large relative influence on the smoothed estimate.

options.label: C
options.text: Dirichlet smoothing adapts by increasing mu automatically for shorter documents and decreasing mu for longer documents, adjusting the pseudo-count at retrieval time based on the length of each individual document being scored.

options.label: D
options.text: Long documents receive heavier smoothing toward the collection model because a larger |d| in the denominator increases the proportion of mu relative to the document's own observed term frequencies in the numerator.

questions.explanationMd: With Dirichlet smoothing, short documents have smaller `|d|`, so the `mu P(t|C)` prior has more relative influence. Longer documents rely more on their own observed term frequencies.

questions.questionMd: What does the Collection Language Model `P(t|C)` represent, and how is it computed according to the Week 7 lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: P(t|C) is the average term frequency of t across all documents, computed by summing tf(t,d) over all documents d and dividing by the number of documents N in the collection.

options.label: B
options.text: P(t|C) is the background probability of term t across the entire corpus, computed as cf(t) / |C|, where cf(t) is the total number of occurrences of t in the collection and |C| is the total token count of the collection.

options.label: C
options.text: P(t|C) is the document frequency proportion of term t, computed as df(t) / N, where df(t) is the number of documents containing t and N is the total number of documents in the entire, whole collection.

options.label: D
options.text: P(t|C) is the inverse document frequency weight for term t, computed as log(N / df(t)), which acts as a proxy for how informative term t is across the entire document collection.

questions.explanationMd: `P(t|C)` is the collection-wide background probability of term `t`. It is computed from collection frequency divided by total token count, not document frequency or IDF.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lab requires students to produce a three-way comparison table for multiple test queries. Which three retrieval configurations are compared, and which evaluation metrics are used?

options.label: A
options.text: The three configurations are MLE query likelihood, Dirichlet-smoothed query likelihood, and Jelinek-Mercer-smoothed query likelihood. Retrieval quality is measured using NDCG@10 and R-Precision on the 20 Newsgroups test queries.

options.label: B
options.text: The three configurations are BM25 baseline, BM25 with Rocchio PRF, and BM25 with RM3 expansion. Retrieval quality is measured using P@10 (precision at rank 10) and MAP (Mean Average Precision) from the Week 5 evaluation pipeline.

options.label: C
options.text: The three configurations are BM25 with WordNet expansion, BM25 with co-occurrence MI expansion, and BM25 with neural Word2Vec expansion. Retrieval quality is measured using P@5 and MRR over a set of 20 manually annotated test queries.

options.label: D
options.text: The three configurations are BM25 baseline, DirichletLM without PRF, and DirichletLM with RM3 expansion. Retrieval quality is measured using Recall@100 and F1@10 computed over the three selected 20 Newsgroups categories.

questions.explanationMd: The lab comparison uses a BM25 baseline and two PRF-based variants: Rocchio PRF and RM3 expansion. The evaluation metrics are P@10 and MAP from the earlier evaluation pipeline.

questions.questionMd: All three smoothing methods taught in Week 7 (Jelinek-Mercer, Dirichlet, and Absolute Discounting) share a common mechanism for preventing zero-probability scores. What is this shared mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: All three methods apply a logarithmic transformation to raw term frequencies before normalization, which compresses zero counts to a very small negative value rather than exactly zero, so the product of per-term scores never reaches the exact value of zero.

options.label: B
options.text: All three methods add a fixed positive constant epsilon to every term's raw count before computing probabilities, ensuring that even terms with tf=0 in a document receive a non-zero numerator and can never produce a zero probability under any parameter settings.

options.label: C
options.text: All three methods remove terms from the query that do not appear in any document in the collection, so the zero-probability problem is pre-empted by filtering the query before scoring, guaranteeing that all remaining query terms have positive document frequencies.

options.label: D
options.text: All three methods mix the document-specific probability estimate with the collection language model P(t|C), which assigns a non-zero probability to every term in the vocabulary, ensuring that unseen query terms always receive a small but positive smoothed probability.

questions.explanationMd: The shared idea behind these smoothing methods is interpolation/backoff to the collection language model. This gives unseen query terms a small non-zero probability as long as they exist in the collection vocabulary.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lab explicitly requires students to find a query where PRF causes retrieval quality to decrease rather than improve. What three things must students document about this failure case, according to the lab instructions?

options.label: A
options.text: Students must identify (a) which specific expansion terms caused the topic drift, (b) why those particular terms appeared in the feedback, i.e. why the initial top-k led to that vocabulary, and (c) what mitigation strategy would reduce the negative impact of expansion for that query.

options.label: B
options.text: Students must document (a) the P@10 score before expansion, (b) the P@10 score after expansion, and (c) the exact expanded query string produced by the PRF algorithm, including all term weights assigned by the Rocchio or RM3 formula.

options.label: C
options.text: Students must document (a) the number of pseudo-relevant documents k used in the feedback step, (b) the number of expansion terms selected from the centroid, and (c) the revised k and m values that would prevent drift without eliminating the expansion benefit for other queries.

options.label: D
options.text: Students must document (a) the original query that caused the failure, (b) the mu value used in the DirichletLM initial retrieval, and (c) a revised mu value that would prevent the failure by reducing the influence of the collection model on the initial top-k result set.

questions.explanationMd: For a PRF failure case, the important analysis is qualitative as well as quantitative: identify the drift terms, explain why the pseudo-relevant set produced them, and propose a mitigation strategy to reduce the negative effect.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is the correct Dirichlet smoothing formula for `P(t|d)` as taught in Week 7, and what is the role of the parameter `μ` in the denominator?

options.label: A
options.text: P_Dir(t|d) = (tf(t,d) + μ × P(t|C)) / (|d| + μ), where μ acts as a pseudo-count of imaginary collection-derived observations added to both the numerator and denominator before normalizing.

options.label: B
options.text: P_Dir(t|d) = max(tf(t,d) - μ, 0) / |d| + μ × |unique_terms(d)| / |d| × P(t|C), where μ is the fixed per-term discount subtracted from all observed frequencies in the document.

options.label: C
options.text: P_Dir(t|d) = tf(t,d) × μ / (|d| × cf(t)), where μ is a scaling factor that amplifies the document term frequency relative to the collection frequency of the same term across all documents.

options.label: D
options.text: P_Dir(t|d) = (1 - μ) P_ML(t|d) + μ P(t|C), where μ in [0,1] linearly interpolates between the document-specific maximum likelihood estimate and the corpus-wide background probability of each term.

questions.explanationMd: Dirichlet smoothing estimates `P(t|d)` by adding `μ × P(t|C)` pseudo-counts from the collection language model and normalizing by `|d| + μ`. Thus, `μ` controls how strongly the document model is pulled toward the collection model.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture describes a geometric interpretation for how the Rocchio algorithm modifies the original query vector. What is this geometric interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: Rocchio scales the query vector by the average retrieval score of the top-k documents, lengthening the query vector in its original direction so that documents similar to the original query receive proportionally higher scores after re-retrieval.

options.label: B
options.text: Rocchio moves the query vector toward the centroid of the pseudo-relevant documents in TF-IDF vector space, so the expanded query q′ is displaced in the direction of the average location of the top-k retrieved documents.

options.label: C
options.text: Rocchio projects the query vector onto the subspace spanned by the pseudo-relevant documents, replacing the original query direction with the component that has the largest cosine similarity to the pseudo-relevant document set.

options.label: D
options.text: Rocchio rotates the query vector by a fixed angle in the direction of the highest-ranked individual document, so the expanded query points toward the single most relevant document rather than toward a centroid of all top-k documents.

questions.explanationMd: Rocchio feedback updates the query by combining the original query with the centroid of pseudo-relevant documents. Geometrically, the query vector moves toward the average position of the top retrieved documents.

questions.questionMd: Which dataset is used in the Week 7 lab, why was it selected, and how are relevance judgments for evaluation produced without manual annotation?

options.label: A
options.text: The TREC Robust04 newswire collection is used because it comes with official NIST relevance judgments that allow students to compute exact evaluation metrics without making any assumptions about which documents count as relevant to each test query.

options.label: B
options.text: The Reuters-21578 dataset from NLTK is used because its 90+ topic categories provide a rich multi-label relevance structure that allows students to evaluate retrieval across many different domain areas within a single standardized document collection.

options.label: C
options.text: The Wikipedia Simple English corpus is used because its short articles closely approximate the average document length that Dirichlet smoothing is optimized for, and its hyperlink structure provides automatic relevance signal for query-document pairs.

options.label: D
options.text: The 20 Newsgroups dataset is used because its category labels serve as pseudo-relevance ground truth: a document is considered relevant to a query if it belongs to the query's target newsgroup category, enabling quantitative P@10 and MAP computation.

questions.explanationMd: The lab uses 20 Newsgroups because its labels can act as pseudo-relevance judgments. If a query is associated with a target category, documents from that category can be treated as relevant for metrics such as P@10 and MAP.

questions.questionMd: Week 7 describes co-occurrence-based query expansion using Mutual Information (MI). What does a high MI value between a candidate term `t` and a query term `q` indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: A high MI value indicates that the document frequency of t is much lower than the document frequency of q, meaning t is a more specific term that can be added to the query to improve precision by restricting results to a narrower part of the collection.

options.label: B
options.text: A high MI value indicates that t appears in a very large proportion of documents in the collection regardless of whether q is present, making t a high-recall expansion term that broadens the query to match many documents across many different topics.

options.label: C
options.text: A high MI value indicates that t and q rarely co-occur in the same documents, suggesting that they refer to complementary aspects of the same topic and that adding t to the query will retrieve documents covering the part of the topic not addressed by q alone.

options.label: D
options.text: A high MI value indicates that t and q co-occur in the collection much more frequently than would be expected by chance if they were independent, suggesting a strong semantic relationship that makes t a good candidate expansion term for queries containing q.

questions.explanationMd: Mutual Information measures association beyond chance. A high MI score means the candidate term and query term co-occur more often than expected under independence, so the candidate term is likely semantically related.

questions.questionMd: A query vector is `q = [1, 0, 1.0]` in a 3-dimensional TF-IDF space. Two pseudo-relevant documents are `d1 = [1, 1, 1]` and `d2 = [0, 1, 1]`. Using Rocchio with `alpha = 1.0` and `beta = 0.75`, what is the expanded query vector `q′`?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the second dimension of q is zero, the Rocchio update ignores that dimension entirely and produces q′ = [1.75, 0, 1.75], treating zero-weighted dimensions in the original query as immutable and preventing any new expansion terms from being added.

options.label: B
options.text: The centroid of d1 and d2 is [0.5, 1.0, 1.0]. Applying the Rocchio formula: q′ = 1.0 × [1, 0, 1] + 0.75 × [0.5, 1.0, 1.0] = [1.375, 0.75, 1.75]. The second dimension becomes positive due to the contribution of 0.75 as a new expansion term.

options.label: C
options.text: The centroid of d1 and d2 is [1.0, 2.0, 2.0] (sum rather than average). Applying the Rocchio formula: q′ = 1.0 × [1, 0, 1] + 0.75 × [1.0, 2.0, 2.0] = [1.75, 1.5, 2.5], overestimating the centroid because the documents were summed instead of averaged.

options.label: D
options.text: The centroid of d1 and d2 is [0.5, 1.0, 1.0]. Applying the Rocchio formula: q′ = 0.75 × [1, 0, 1] + 1.0 × [0.5, 1.0, 1.0] = [1.25, 1.0, 1.75]. The alpha and beta roles are swapped, giving the centroid a higher weight than the original query vector.

questions.explanationMd: The pseudo-relevant centroid is the average of `d1` and `d2`: `[0.5, 1.0, 1.0]`. Rocchio gives `q′ = αq + β centroid = [1,0,1] + 0.75[0.5,1,1] = [1.375,0.75,1.75]`.

questions.questionMd: Two pseudo-relevant documents are retrieved for query `space`. Doc A with `P(A|q) = 0.6` has `P("shuttle"|A) = 0.10`, and Doc B with `P(B|q) = 0.4` has `P("shuttle"|B) = 0.04`. What is `P("shuttle"|R)` according to the RM1 formula?

options.label: A
options.text: P("shuttle"|R) = 0.10 × 0.4 + 0.04 × 0.6 = 0.04 + 0.024 = 0.064. The relevance weights P(d|q) are swapped between the two documents, assigning the higher weight to the document that scores lower in the initial retrieval ranking.

options.label: B
options.text: P("shuttle"|R) = 0.10 × 0.6 + 0.04 × 0.4 = 0.06 + 0.016 = 0.076. Doc A contributes more because it both assigns a higher probability to "shuttle" and receives a higher relevance weight from the initial query scoring.

options.label: C
options.text: P("shuttle"|R) = max(0.10 × 0.6, 0.04 × 0.4) = max(0.06, 0.016) = 0.06. Only the contribution from the highest-ranked document is used, and the lower-ranked document's probability mass is completely discarded from the computation.

options.label: D
options.text: P("shuttle"|R) = (0.10 + 0.04) / 2 = 0.07. The two document probabilities are averaged with equal weight, ignoring the different query-conditioned relevance scores assigned to each document by the initial retrieval model.

questions.explanationMd: RM1 estimates the relevance model by summing term probabilities weighted by each document's query-conditioned relevance. Therefore `0.10 × 0.6 + 0.04 × 0.4 = 0.076`.

questions.explanationMd: Polysemy occurs when one word has multiple meanings. Global thesaurus expansion may choose synonyms from the wrong sense, causing topic drift and reduced precision; filtering ambiguous or high-frequency terms is one mitigation.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture contrasts document expansion with query expansion as strategies for addressing vocabulary mismatch. What is the primary practical reason that query expansion is generally preferred over document expansion in production retrieval systems?

options.label: A
options.text: Document expansion requires access to the original document authors to obtain approved synonyms for the content they wrote, whereas query expansion can be performed automatically without any involvement from the creators of the indexed documents.

options.label: B
options.text: Query expansion produces consistently higher precision and recall than document expansion on all known benchmark collections, because adding terms to the query is a mathematically optimal strategy that cannot be matched by the heuristic approach of modifying stored documents.

options.label: C
options.text: Query expansion adds terms at search time without modifying the index, making it much cheaper to deploy and update, whereas document expansion requires re-indexing the entire collection every time the expansion vocabulary or policy changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Query expansion allows the system to use a different set of expansion terms for every individual query term in every document, whereas document expansion must apply a single uniform synonym dictionary to all terms in all documents at the time of indexing.

questions.explanationMd: Query expansion is operationally easier because it changes only the query-processing step. Document expansion modifies stored documents or the index, so vocabulary-policy changes may require expensive re-indexing.

questions.questionMd: What is the Bayesian interpretation of the `μ` parameter in Dirichlet smoothing, as explained in the Week 7 lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: μ represents the maximum a posteriori estimate of the document length, used to normalize the smoothed term probabilities so that they sum to exactly one across all terms in the vocabulary of the collection.

options.label: B
options.text: μ represents the number of pseudo-observations drawn from the collection model that are added to the document before observing the actual document tokens.

options.label: C
options.text: μ represents the posterior variance of the collection language model, quantifying how uncertain the model is about the true term probabilities in the collection before any document-specific observations are incorporated.

options.label: D
options.text: μ represents the number of documents in the collection that are assumed to be a priori relevant to any query, functioning as a relevance prior that up-weights collection-frequent terms before document scoring begins.

questions.explanationMd: Under a Bayesian interpretation, `μ` is the strength of the prior: it acts like a number of pseudo-observations sampled from the collection language model and mixed with the document's observed counts.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture draws a connection between the statistical language model framework and modern neural language models. Which statement correctly describes this connection as it is presented in the course materials?

options.label: A
options.text: The RM3 relevance model formula is the statistical predecessor to the cross-attention layer in BERT-based neural rerankers, since both methods compute a weighted combination of individual document term probabilities conditioned on an initial query representation.

options.label: B
options.text: The Rocchio algorithm in TF-IDF vector space is functionally identical to a single gradient descent update in a neural retrieval model, because both methods move a query representation in the direction of a pseudo-relevant centroid by a fixed learning rate.

options.label: C
options.text: The same n-gram language model framework introduced this week underpins GPT pretraining objectives and speech recognition systems, making the classical probabilistic formulation a direct conceptual precursor to modern language models.

options.label: D
options.text: The Dirichlet-smoothed language model is mathematically equivalent to the attention mechanism in transformer-based neural language models, because both compute a weighted sum over context tokens using a softmax-normalized distribution.

questions.explanationMd: Classical n-gram language models introduced the probabilistic idea of modeling sequences with term probabilities. Modern neural language models such as GPT use much richer architectures, but they still build on the language-modeling objective.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture describes **selective expansion** as a strategy for global query expansion using thesauri. What does selective expansion mean in this context, and why is it used?

options.label: A
options.text: Selective expansion means choosing the single highest-MI expansion term from the co-occurrence statistics and adding only that one term to the query, rather than adding all candidate synonyms, to prevent the query from becoming so long that term independence assumptions break down.

options.label: B
options.text: Selective expansion means applying thesaurus-based expansion only to query terms where initial retrieval confidence is low, rather than expanding all query terms indiscriminately, to avoid degrading precision for terms that are already retrieving relevant documents effectively.

options.label: C
options.text: Selective expansion means expanding only queries that contain fewer than three terms, because short queries benefit most from additional vocabulary while long queries already contain sufficient discriminative terms to retrieve relevant documents without any expansion.

options.label: D
options.text: Selective expansion means expanding query terms only when the term appears in fewer than 1% of collection documents, because extremely rare terms are the ones most likely to suffer from vocabulary mismatch and therefore most in need of synonym-based support.

questions.explanationMd: Selective expansion avoids expanding every query term blindly. It applies expansion only where the original retrieval signal is weak, which helps reduce query drift and prevents precision loss for terms that already retrieve relevant documents well.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture compares the Rocchio algorithm to the RM3 relevance model. Which of the following correctly describes a key difference between the two PRF approaches?

options.label: A
options.text: Rocchio consistently outperforms RM3 on TREC benchmarks because TF-IDF vector space is a more accurate representation of term importance than probabilistic language model scores derived from Dirichlet-smoothed document models.

options.label: B
options.text: Rocchio is a probabilistic model that derives expansion terms by computing relevance language model probabilities, whereas RM3 is a geometric model that moves the query vector in TF-IDF space toward the centroid of pseudo-relevant documents.

options.label: C
options.text: Rocchio operates geometrically in TF-IDF vector space, moving the query toward the pseudo-relevant centroid, whereas RM3 is probabilistically grounded and weights each document's contribution by its query-conditioned relevance probability using language model scores.

options.label: D
options.text: Rocchio requires explicit relevance judgments from human assessors to compute the non-relevant document centroid, whereas RM3 is fully automatic and uses only the top-k retrieved documents without requiring any manual relevance assessment.

questions.explanationMd: Rocchio is a vector-space feedback method: it moves the query vector toward the centroid of pseudo-relevant documents. RM3 is a language-model-based PRF method that estimates expansion term probabilities using document language models weighted by query-conditioned relevance probabilities.

questions.questionMd: A student's DirichletLM implementation produces a score of negative infinity (`-inf`) for certain queries against some documents. According to the Week 7 troubleshooting guide, what is the cause and the recommended fix?

options.label: A
options.text: The mu parameter is set to zero, collapsing the Dirichlet formula to the raw MLE estimate, which then assigns zero probability to unseen query terms and produces a log of zero error during the summation of log term probabilities in the scoring function.

options.label: B
options.text: The `bm25.search()` function is returning document objects rather than integer indices, causing an `IndexError` when the `pseudo_rel_ids` are used to slice the TF-IDF matrix `X`, and the `IndexError` is being incorrectly caught and converted to a `-inf` score by the exception handler.

options.label: C
options.text: A query term has zero probability in the collection model, causing `log(0)` when computing the log-sum score. The fix is to add a small floor value such as `1e-10` to the `p_collection()` function so that no term ever returns an exact zero probability.

options.label: D
options.text: The Rocchio expansion terms are only stop words because `stop_words='english'` was not set in the `TfidfVectorizer`, causing the expanded query to contain only high-frequency function words that have near-zero IDF weights and produce trivially low log scores.

questions.explanationMd: A `-inf` log-likelihood usually appears when a probability becomes exactly zero and the implementation computes `log(0)`. Adding a small floor to the collection probability avoids zero probabilities and keeps the log-score finite.

questions.questionMd: The RM1 relevance model computes `P(t|R)`, the probability of term `t` given the pseudo-relevant set `R`. Which formula correctly describes this computation as taught in Week 7?

options.label: A
options.text: `P(t|R) = (1/|R|) × sum` over all documents `d` in the top-k set of `P(t|d)`, where the term probability in each pseudo-relevant document is simply averaged with equal weight regardless of how relevant each document is to the query.

options.label: B
options.text: `P(t|R) = sum` over all documents `d` in the top-k set of `[P(t|d) × P(d|q)]`, where each document's language model probability for term `t` is weighted by that document's query-conditioned relevance probability.

options.label: C
options.text: `P(t|R) = max` over all documents `d` in the top-k set of `[P(t|d) × P(d|q)]`, where only the single most relevant document's contribution is used to assign an expansion term probability rather than aggregating across all pseudo-relevant documents.

options.label: D
options.text: `P(t|R) = P(t|C) × sum` over all documents `d` in the top-k set of `P(d|q)`, where the collection-level term probability is scaled by the total probability mass assigned to the pseudo-relevant documents by the initial retrieval model.

questions.explanationMd: RM1 estimates the relevance model by aggregating term probabilities from pseudo-relevant documents. Each document contributes according to `P(d|q)`, so documents that are more likely to be relevant to the query have greater influence on `P(t|R)`.

questions.questionMd: The Rocchio algorithm for Pseudo-Relevance Feedback uses a formula to compute the expanded query vector `q'`. In the PRF setting where no explicit non-relevant documents are available, which formula correctly represents the Rocchio update as taught in Week 7?

options.label: A
options.text: `q' = alpha × q + beta × (1/|Rel|) × sum of d for all d in Rel`, where alpha and beta weight the original query and the pseudo-relevant document centroid respectively, and the gamma non-relevant term drops out.

options.label: B
options.text: `q' = alpha × q - gamma × (1/|NR|) × sum of d for all d in NR`, where the original query is preserved at weight alpha and the centroid of non-relevant documents is subtracted with weight gamma to move the query away from off-topic content.

options.label: C
options.text: `q' = (1 - lambda) × P_RM1(t) + lambda × P_ML(t|q)`, where lambda controls the balance between expansion terms derived from the top-k relevance model and the original maximum likelihood query term probabilities.

options.label: D
options.text: `q' = sum over all d in Rel of [P(t|d) × P(d|q)]`, where each document's contribution to the new query vector is weighted by the posterior probability of relevance given the original query terms and document scores.

questions.explanationMd: In the PRF version of Rocchio, the system has pseudo-relevant documents but no explicit non-relevant set. Therefore, the update keeps the original query vector and adds the centroid of pseudo-relevant documents, while the non-relevant subtraction term is omitted.

questions.questionMd: A two-term query `q = {"orbit", "launch"}` is scored against document `d`, which contains `"orbit"` three times but does not contain `"launch"` at all. Under the unsmoothed query likelihood model using MLE, what is the resulting score `P(q|d)`?

options.label: A
options.text: The score is very small but non-zero, because MLE automatically falls back to the collection probability `P(t|C)` whenever a term is absent from a document, preventing the score from reaching zero.

options.label: B
options.text: The score equals `P("orbit"|d)`, because missing terms are simply ignored in the product formula and the non-zero term probabilities are multiplied together over the subset of terms that do appear in the document.

options.label: C
options.text: The score is exactly 0, because `P("launch"|d) = 0` under MLE, and multiplying any non-zero probability by zero in the product `P("orbit"|d) × P("launch"|d)` forces the entire query likelihood to zero.

options.label: D
options.text: The score is undefined and the document is excluded from ranking entirely, because a document that is missing any query term is considered completely irrelevant by the query likelihood model.

questions.explanationMd: With unsmoothed MLE, a term absent from a document has probability zero. Since query likelihood multiplies the probabilities of query terms, one missing term makes the whole product zero.

questions.questionMd: What is the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) for the probability of term `t` given document `d`, as defined in the Week 7 lectures?

options.label: A
options.text: `P_ML(t|d) = cf(t) / |C|`, where `cf(t)` is the collection frequency of term `t` and `|C|` is the total number of tokens in the entire corpus collection.

options.label: B
options.text: `P_ML(t|d) = tf(t,d) / |d|`, where `tf(t,d)` is the number of times term `t` appears in document `d` and `|d|` is the total number of tokens in document `d`.

options.label: C
options.text: `P_ML(t|d) = tf(t,d) / df(t)`, where `tf(t,d)` is the term frequency in document `d` and `df(t)` is the number of documents in the collection that contain term `t`.

options.label: D
options.text: `P_ML(t|d) = log(tf(t,d) + 1) / |d|`, where the logarithm is applied to dampen the effect of high-frequency terms before dividing by the document length.

questions.explanationMd: The document MLE estimates a term's probability from its observed relative frequency inside that document: term count divided by total document length.

questions.questionMd: According to the Week 7 materials, what is the significance of RM3 in the context of academic IR evaluation systems, and which toolkit provides a standard RM3 implementation that students are suggested to use for the exercise course project?

options.label: C
options.text: RM3 is a proprietary algorithm developed by Google that has only recently been made available for academic use, and scikit-learn provides the standard open-source implementation that students use in the Week 7 lab and in their course project submissions.

options.label: D

questions.questionMd: In the RM3 formula `P_RM3(t) = (1 - lambda) × P_RM1(t) + lambda × P_ML(t|q)`, what happens to the expanded query when lambda is set close to 1.0, and when is this setting advisable?

options.label: A
options.text: When lambda is close to 1.0, the RM3 model heavily emphasizes the original query term probabilities and gives very little weight to expansion terms from the relevance model. This setting is advisable when topic drift is a concern or when initial retrieval precision is low.

options.label: B
options.text: When lambda is close to 1.0, the Dirichlet smoothing parameter mu is implicitly increased within the RM3 pipeline, causing the pseudo-relevant document language models to converge toward the collection model and reducing the distinctiveness of each document's expansion contribution.

options.label: C
options.text: When lambda is close to 1.0, the RM3 formula becomes equivalent to the Rocchio formula, because both methods then assign equal weight to all documents in the pseudo-relevant set and compute an unweighted average of per-term probabilities across the top-k feedback documents.

options.label: D
options.text: When lambda is close to 1.0, the RM3 model fully replaces the original query with the expansion terms from `P_RM1(t)` and ignores the original query entirely. This setting is advisable when the initial retrieval returns many highly relevant documents in the top-k positions.

questions.explanationMd: In RM3, lambda controls interpolation with the original query model. Values near 1.0 keep the expanded query close to the original query, which can reduce topic drift when feedback documents may not be reliable.

questions.questionMd: A student claims: "Setting mu to a very large value in Dirichlet smoothing reduces the influence of the collection model and makes the score rely more on the document's own term frequencies." Is this claim correct, and what actually happens as mu increases toward infinity?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct. Larger mu amplifies the weight of the document's own term frequencies in the numerator, causing the smoothed estimate to move progressively closer to the raw MLE value and further from the collection model.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is irrelevant because the optimal mu is a fixed universal constant of 1500 for all retrieval collections, so practitioners should never adjust it based on collection-specific properties or document length distributions and the net effect on ranking depends entirely on the average document length in the collection.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is partially correct. Larger mu reduces smoothing only for long documents while simultaneously increasing smoothing for short documents, so the net effect on ranking depends entirely on the average document length in the collection.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is incorrect. Larger mu means MORE smoothing toward the collection model. As mu approaches infinity, the document-specific term frequencies become negligible and all documents converge to the same collection-wide probability distribution, making ranking useless.

questions.explanationMd: Dirichlet smoothing interpolates document evidence with collection evidence. Increasing `mu` gives more weight to the collection model; in the limit, document-specific counts vanish and all documents look the same under the collection distribution.

questions.questionMd: In the context of information retrieval as taught in Week 7, how is a language model used to rank documents in response to a query?

options.label: A
options.text: Each query is modelled as a probability distribution over vocabulary terms, and documents are ranked by the probability that the query's language model would generate the words found in each document.

options.label: B
options.text: Each document is modelled as a probability distribution over vocabulary terms, and documents are ranked by the probability that the document's language model would generate the observed query words.

options.label: C
options.text: Each document is modelled as a Markov chain over word sequences, and documents are ranked by the joint probability of generating the entire query sentence in the correct left-to-right word order.

options.label: D
options.text: A single collection-wide language model is trained, and documents are ranked by how much their term frequencies deviate from the predictions made by that unified collection model.

questions.explanationMd: In the query likelihood model, every document has its own language model. A document receives a high score if its model assigns high probability to the query terms.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture draws a connection between the statistical language model framework and modern neural language models. Which statement correctly describes this connection as it is presented in the course materials?

options.label: A
options.text: The Dirichlet-smoothed language model is mathematically equivalent to the attention mechanism in transformer-based neural language models, because both compute a weighted sum over context tokens using a softmax-normalized distribution.

options.label: B
options.text: The same n-gram language model framework introduced this week underpins GPT pretraining objectives and speech recognition systems, making the classical probabilistic formulation a direct conceptual precursor to modern large language models.

options.label: C
options.text: The Rocchio algorithm in TF-IDF vector space is functionally identical to a single gradient descent update in a neural retrieval model, because both methods move a query representation in the direction of a pseudo-relevant centroid by a fixed learning rate.

options.label: D
options.text: The RM3 relevance model formula is the statistical predecessor to the cross-attention layer in BERT-based neural rerankers, since both methods compute a weighted combination of individual document term probabilities conditioned on an initial query representation.

questions.explanationMd: Classical n-gram language models introduced the idea of assigning probabilities to word sequences. Modern neural language models generalize this idea with neural representations and larger contexts.

questions.questionMd: The Week 7 lecture uses the query `jaguar` to illustrate topic drift during PRF. Which scenario correctly describes how topic drift manifests for this query?

options.label: A
options.text: If the initial top-k results are dominated by automotive reviews, the expansion terms will be concepts like `horsepower`, `engine`, and `sedan`, causing the re-retrieved results to further emphasize the car sense of `jaguar` and crowd out wildlife or other relevant documents.

options.label: B
options.text: The WordNet thesaurus assigns `jaguar` to a single unambiguous synset covering only the animal sense, so all expansion terms from the thesaurus refer to wildlife, and the RM3 model fails to find documents about Jaguar cars regardless of the initial retrieval results.

options.label: C
options.text: The Dirichlet smoothing parameter mu is set too low for the `jaguar` query, causing the initial retrieval to assign zero probability to any automotive-related terms and preventing the PRF system from finding any meaningful expansion terms at all.

options.label: D
options.text: If the initial top-k results are dominated by wildlife articles, the expansion terms will be concepts like `prey`, `habitat`, and `feline`, which are highly specific synonyms that narrow the query to only wildlife documents and exclude many other relevant automotive sources.

questions.explanationMd: Topic drift happens when feedback terms reflect the dominant sense in the initial results instead of the user's intended sense. For `jaguar`, car-heavy results can push the expanded query further toward cars.

questions.questionMd: A query vector is `q = [1.0, 0, 1.0]` in a 3-dimensional TF-IDF space. Two pseudo-relevant documents are `d1 = [1, 1, 1]` and `d2 = [0, 1, 1]`. Using Rocchio with `alpha = 1.0` and `beta = 0.75`, what is the expanded query vector `q'`?

options.label: A
options.text: The centroid of d1 and d2 is [1.0, 2.0, 2.0] rather than their average. Applying the Rocchio formula `q' = 1.0 × [1, 0, 1] + 0.75 × [1.0, 2.0, 2.0] = [1.75, 1.5, 2.5]`, overestimating the centroid because the documents were summed instead of averaged.

options.label: B
options.text: The centroid of d1 and d2 is [0.5, 1.0, 1.0]. Applying the Rocchio formula `q' = 1.0 × [1, 0, 1] + 0.75 × [0.5, 1.0, 1.0] = [1.375, 0.75, 1.75]`. The second dimension, previously zero, now has a positive weight of 0.75 as an expansion term.

options.label: C
options.text: The centroid of d1 and d2 is [0.5, 1.0, 1.0]. Applying the Rocchio formula `q' = 0.75 × [1, 0, 1] + 1.0 × [0.5, 1.0, 1.0] = [1.25, 1.0, 1.75]`. The alpha and beta values are swapped, giving the centroid a higher weight than the original query vector.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the second dimension of q is zero, Rocchio update ignores that dimension entirely and produces `q' = [1.375, 0, 1.75]`, treating zero-weighted dimensions in the original query as immutable and preventing any new expansion terms from being added.

questions.explanationMd: Rocchio uses `q' = alpha q + beta centroid(D_r)`. The centroid is `[0.5, 1.0, 1.0]`, so `q' = [1,0,1] + 0.75[0.5,1,1] = [1.375,0.75,1.75]`.

questions.questionMd: The Query Likelihood Retrieval Model scores a document `d` for query `q`. Given that query term `t` appears `tf(t,q)` times in `q` and the model assigns probability `P(t|d)` to each term, which formula correctly expresses the query likelihood score in log form?

options.label: A
options.text: `log P(q|d) = sum over all terms t in q of [log P(t|d) - log P(t|C)]`, which measures the divergence between the document model and the collection model as a sum of log-ratio terms over all query terms.

options.label: B
options.text: `log P(q|d) = product over all terms t in q of [P(t|d) / P(t|C)]`, which normalizes each document-level probability by the baseline collection probability before multiplying the ratios together into a final score.

options.label: C
options.text: `log P(q|d) = sum over all terms t in q of [tf(t,d) × log P(t|C)]`, which weights the collection-level probability of each term by how often that term appears in the document rather than in the query.

options.label: D
options.text: `log P(q|d) = sum over all terms t in q of [tf(t,q) × log P(t|d)]`, which converts the product of per-term probabilities into a sum of log probabilities to avoid floating-point underflow during computation.

questions.explanationMd: The query likelihood score multiplies document-model probabilities for the query terms. In log space, this becomes a weighted sum using query term frequencies.

questions.questionMd: Which formula correctly describes Jelinek-Mercer (JM) smoothing as presented in the Week 7 lecture, and what does the parameter lambda control?

options.label: A
options.text: `P_JM(t|d) = (tf(t,d) + lambda × P(t|C)) / (|d| + lambda)`, where lambda is a pseudo-count that adds imaginary collection-derived pseudo-observations to the document's own observed term counts before normalization.

options.label: B
options.text: `P_JM(t|d) = (1 - lambda) × P_ML(t|d) + lambda × P(t|C)`, where `lambda` in `[0,1]` controls the linear interpolation balance between the document-specific MLE estimate and the collection-wide probability.

options.label: C
options.text: `P_JM(t|d) = tf(t,d) / |d| + lambda × df(t)`, where lambda scales a document-frequency penalty that reduces the weight of terms appearing in many documents throughout the collection.

options.label: D
options.text: `P_JM(t|d) = max(tf(t,d) - lambda, 0) / |d| + lambda × |unique_terms(d)| / |d| × P(t|C)`, where lambda is the fixed discount subtracted from every observed term count in the document.

questions.explanationMd: JM smoothing linearly interpolates the document maximum-likelihood model with the collection model. Lambda determines how much probability mass is taken from the collection model.

questions.questionMd: According to Week 7, under what conditions does PRF reliably help retrieval, and under what conditions does it reliably hurt?

options.label: A
options.text: PRF reliably helps when the initial retrieval precision is already above 0.5, meaning most top-k documents are genuinely on-topic; PRF reliably hurts for ambiguous short queries of one or two words and for queries in specialized domains poorly represented in the collection.

options.label: B
options.text: PRF reliably helps when the query contains many rare terms that are absent from most documents in the collection; PRF reliably hurts when the query contains only common, high-frequency terms that already match a large proportion of the document collection.

options.label: C
options.text: PRF reliably helps when the Dirichlet mu parameter is set above 2000, giving the initial retrieval a strong collection-level smoothing signal; PRF reliably hurts when mu is set below 500, causing the initial top-k to be dominated by short documents with inflated term frequencies.

options.label: D
options.text: PRF reliably helps when the number of pseudo-relevant documents k is set above 50 so the centroid averages out noisy individual documents; PRF reliably hurts when k is set to fewer than 5, leaving the centroid dominated by a single document's idiosyncratic vocabulary.

questions.explanationMd: PRF assumes the top results are mostly relevant. If that assumption is true, feedback terms help; if the query is ambiguous or the initial ranking is poor, feedback can drift away from the intended topic.
